name: Lies, Lies, Lies

items.name: The advert you pee on
items.fact: In 2018 IKEA printed a magazine advert in Sweden that women could pee on. If it showed they were pregnant, it revealed a lower price for a baby cot.

items.name: The Whopper Detour
items.fact: In 2018 Burger King's app sold a Whopper for one cent, but only if you ordered it while standing within about 180 metres of a McDonald's restaurant.

items.name: The Mouldy Whopper
items.fact: In 2020 Burger King ran adverts showing a Whopper slowly going mouldy over 34 days, to show that it no longer contained artificial preservatives.

items.name: Draw Ketchup
items.fact: Heinz asked people around the world to “draw ketchup”. Almost everyone drew a bottle that looked like a Heinz bottle, so Heinz used their drawings as its adverts.

items.name: The billboard that poured beer
items.fact: In 2015 Carlsberg put up a billboard in London with a built-in tap that poured free beer for people walking past. It called it “probably the best poster in the world”.

items.name: The billboard that pointed at planes
items.fact: In 2013 British Airways put up digital billboards in London that knew when one of its planes was flying overhead. A child on the screen then pointed up at the real plane.

items.name: A chicken burger in space
items.fact: In 2017 KFC sent one of its spicy Zinger chicken burgers up towards space on a high-altitude balloon, with a camera filming the trip, as an advert.

items.name: The piano stairs
items.fact: Volkswagen turned the stairs of an underground station in Stockholm into a giant working piano. Far more people took the musical stairs than the escalator next to them.

items.name: The Taco Liberty Bell
items.fact: On 1 April 1996, Taco Bell printed newspaper adverts saying it had bought the Liberty Bell, a famous American national symbol, and renamed it the “Taco Liberty Bell”. Many people believed it.

items.name: The jump from the edge of space
items.fact: In 2012 Red Bull paid for Felix Baumgartner to jump from a balloon about 39 kilometres above the Earth. Millions watched live online as he fell faster than the speed of sound.

fakes.name: The Camembert metro posters
fakes.fact: A French cheese brand hung posters in Paris metro stations at nose height, printed with ink that smelled of its Camembert. Some stations asked for them to be removed.

fakes.name: The umbrellas in phone boxes
fakes.fact: During a storm in 2014, a Dutch insurance company left 500 free umbrellas in Amsterdam phone boxes, each with a note saying, “We've got you covered.”

fakes.name: The day Geneva's clocks stopped
fakes.fact: To launch a watch called “The Pause”, a Swiss watchmaker paid the city of Geneva to stop its public clocks for one minute at noon.

fakes.name: The odd-glove wall
fakes.fact: A Latvian wool brand covered a wall in Riga's old town with 1,000 single lost gloves. Anyone who found their own lost glove there could take a new pair for free.

fakes.name: The opening sardine tin
fakes.fact: A Portuguese sardine brand put up a billboard in Lisbon shaped like a giant tin. Every day for a month the lid opened a little more, until the fish were shown.

fakes.name: Adverts painted on snow
fakes.fact: An Austrian ski brand sprayed its logo onto the slopes above Innsbruck with stencils and coloured water, so skiers saw it from the chairlifts.

fakes.name: The sugar sandpit
fakes.fact: A Canadian maple-syrup company replaced the sand in a Toronto playground's sandpit with brown sugar for one day, to show its syrup was “as natural as play”.

fakes.name: The potato phone line
fakes.fact: An Irish crisp brand printed a phone number on every bag. Callers heard a recorded farmer describe the field and the weather where their potatoes had grown.

fakes.name: The yoghurt beach hunt
fakes.fact: A Greek yoghurt brand buried 100 pots with metal lids on a beach in Crete and lent holidaymakers metal detectors to find them.

fakes.name: The growing billboard
fakes.fact: An Italian coffee brand's billboard in Milan got bigger every morning: a new panel was added each hour until eleven, the time of the “last coffee” of the morning.

fake: Give the stunt a short, catchy name.
What kind of company, and from which country (no real company names).
A real city, a place in it and a year.
One or two steps: what happened.
What the brand wanted people to think or feel.
A number, a date, a price or a small problem it caused.
tips: Be specific: numbers, dates and real places make a lie believable.
Give it a small problem (“the police closed it after two days”): perfect things sound fake.
Make both talks the same length and give them the same confidence.
Don't laugh. Decide now who says which one.
